title: Activist Sonam Wangchuk Ends 26-Day Hunger Strike as India's 'Cockroach' Protest Movement Intensifies
excerpt: The 59-year-old Ladakhi activist broke his fast after government ministers visited him in hospital, but the youth-led movement demanding the education minister's resignation shows no sign of stopping.
body:
• Sonam Wangchuk, 59, ended his 26-day hunger strike on Friday after senior BJP ministers visited him in hospital and pledged not to file cases against peaceful protesters.
  • India's Cockroach Janta Party says protests will continue until Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns over the NEET medical exam paper leak scandal.
  • Tens of thousands of young people have converged on Delhi in what the Wall Street Journal calls the biggest youth challenge to PM Modi since he came to power in 2014.
  • The government has asked for time until Saturday to respond to the demand for the minister's resignation.

Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike on Friday after two senior government ministers visited him at Medanta Hospital in Gurugram and offered a set of concessions, but the youth-led protest movement he helped energize is showing no signs of retreat.

"Just now in the presence of Union Ministers J.P. Nadda, Dr. Jitendra Singh and the senior leaders of Apex Body of Leh Ladakh, I finally broke my fast after 26 days," Wangchuk said in a post on X. The 59-year-old Ladakhi activist, who lost roughly 20 pounds during the fast, said the decision came "after a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country."

What the Government Offered

Health Minister J.P. Nadda, reading out the government's commitments to Wangchuk at his bedside, said the administration would not register criminal cases against those who protested peacefully at Jantar Mantar or participated in the march to Parliament on July 20. The government also said it was "positively considering suitable compensation for the suicide victims of recent NEET paper leaks."

https://x.com/ajplus/status/2080685186090766442

A video posted by Wangchuk showed government officials lined up along his hospital bed — a striking image in a country where such concessions from the ruling BJP are rare.

Prime Minister Modi responded on social media: "I urge Sonam ji to follow his daily routine as advised by the doctors and regain his weight as soon as possible. I pray to the Almighty that Sonam ji remains healthy."

The Cockroach Movement Keeps Growing

Despite Wangchuk's decision to end his fast, the Cockroach Janta Party — the self-named youth movement at the heart of the protests — said Friday it would not back down.

"We will not step back. By putting your own life on the line, you awakened the conscience of an entire nation."

— Abhijeet Dipke, Founder, Cockroach Janta Party

The movement's central demand remains the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the botched NEET undergraduate medical entrance exam. The test, taken by two million students in May, was canceled and retaken in June after exam papers were leaked. Several families have paid tens of thousands of dollars for advance access to papers through organized cheating rings, according to the Wall Street Journal.

In India, competitive exams are the gateway for millions to subsidized college spots or government jobs amid a shortage of well-paying private employment. The NEET scandal hit particularly hard because the exam determines admission to medical schools — a path many Indian families view as the cornerstone of upward mobility, both at home and for those seeking to study or practice abroad.

Biggest Youth Challenge to Modi

The protests represent what the Wall Street Journal described as the biggest youth challenge to Prime Minister Modi since he came to power in 2014. Opposition parties have echoed the movement's demands and disrupted the monsoon session of Parliament that began this week.

On Monday, police banned a planned protest march on Parliament but thousands turned out anyway. Clashes with police resulted in dozens of protesters injured, while authorities said nearly 120 police and paramilitary personnel were also hurt.

The movement has drawn remarkable cross-community solidarity. Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs have worked together to distribute food and water at protest sites. Indians across the country have used food delivery apps to send meals to protest sites with messages like "love from Kerala." Teenagers have traveled from distant towns, and some couples brought their children to witness the demonstrations.

Government Seeks More Time

Following the first substantive talks between protest leaders and the government on Friday — represented by ministers Nadda and Jitendra Singh on the government side, and CJP spokespersons Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on the protest side — the government asked for time until Saturday afternoon to respond on the central demand for Pradhan's resignation.

"We hope the government will dismiss Dharmendra Pradhan at the earliest, or that he will resign, so that we can bring this matter to a conclusion," Ranka told reporters after the meeting. The CJP has called for nationwide protests on Friday in solidarity with students who faced police action.
nri_angle: The Cockroach movement has drawn global attention to India's competitive exam crisis, which directly shapes the pipeline of Indian students seeking US university spots and eventually H-1B visas.
